writing.exampleCaption: Position for a tuple, index for an array.
writing.explanation:
Tuples group a fixed number of possibly different types and are read by position. Arrays hold one type with a length known at compile time, which is exactly what lets the compiler bounds-check them and reject an out-of-range index it can see.

The `point` in the example is a tuple: its first field is an `i32` and its second is an `f64`. The fields are read as `point.0` and `point.1` because their positions, not names, identify them. The `scores` array is different: all four elements are `u8`, and the length `4` belongs to the type `[u8; 4]`. That makes `scores[2]` a predictable access to the third score. Before using an index, ask whether the index is a constant the compiler can reject or a runtime value that needs a check.

Tuples help when a few values belong together for a short journey through code. Arrays help when you have a fixed-size sequence of one kind of item. Neither is a general substitute for a struct with meaningful field names or a `Vec` that must grow. Choosing the shape is part of explaining the data, not merely satisfying syntax. In a function signature, `(i32, f64)` tells callers exactly what comes back, while `[u8; 4]` promises exactly four scores.

Try changing the tuple field order and observe which accesses now need a different type. Then change the array length annotation without changing its elements. Compare the two diagnostics: one concerns the type at a position, the other concerns the number of elements. Predict whether an out-of-range constant index will be caught before execution, and distinguish that case from an index read from user input.

A type annotation can document intent at a public boundary or resolve an otherwise ambiguous parse. Inside a small expression, inference usually keeps the code lighter. Add annotations where they help the reader or compiler choose, not mechanically to every binding.

A type tells the compiler which operations a value supports and how it is represented. `i32` is a signed 32-bit integer, `bool` is `true` or `false`, and `&str` is borrowed UTF-8 text. A tuple groups values by position; an array stores a fixed number of values of one element type. Read a type annotation from the inside out instead of trying to memorize every symbol at once. For `[i32; 3]`, the element type is `i32` and the length is three.

Inference works when the surrounding code gives enough information, but an explicit annotation can document intent or settle ambiguity. Try changing a tuple element from a number to text and see which later operations stop compiling. Then compare an array with a `Vec`: an array's length is part of its type, while a vector can grow. When a type error appears, find the expression that produces the value and the place that expects it. The difference between those two is the decision you need to make.
writing.feedback: A constant index past a known length is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.

recall.question: Why is this declaration rejected even though every element is a valid `u8`?
recall.answer: The length is part of an array's type. `[u8; 4]` promises exactly four elements, but the literal has three, so rustc reports mismatched types (E0308) about the element count, not the element type.

recall.question: Why must a tuple field be accessed as `point.0` and not `point[i]` with a variable index, while an array allows `scores[i]`?
recall.answer: Tuple fields can have different types, so the compiler must know the position to know the type; `point[0]` is rejected with E0608. An array holds one element type, so an index computed at runtime still yields a known type.
